Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Kai, a 42-year-old electrician of Māori descent, worked nights repairing electrical panels in the high-rise condos of the city. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, when the sun was at its zenith and the building's air-conditioning unit whirred, he was at his home, listening to his wife's voice through the kitchen window as she prepared dinner. The quiet was shattered when the front door suddenly slammed shut with a heavy, violent thud, and a masked figure rushed inside, brandishing a knife. Kai's heart pounded; he could feel the metal weight of the blade pressed against his ribs. The intruder lunged, and in an instant the world became a blur of darkness and terror. Kai managed to push the assailant into the basement crawl-space, but the man was not stopped; he dragged Kai out, slashing his left wrist. When the police arrived, the attacker fled, leaving Kai in shock, blood dripping from his wound, the taste of metal lingering in his mouth. The time of that day-3:15 p.m.-became forever etched in his mind as the exact moment the life he knew was ripped apart. In the days that followed, Kai found that the clock's hands at 3:15 p.m. pulled him back into the assault. The minute the second hand reached that number, his mind snapped into that violent flash, his skin prickled with a dissociative feeling, and he felt as if he were watching the scene from outside himself. The abrupt slam of a door in a quiet house or the sudden clatter of a neighbor's refrigerator on the other side of the wall would trigger the same disorienting surge. Each time a door opened, the memory of the intruder's breath on his ear resurfaced, and he felt the weight of the knife's edge in his chest. Those triggers pushed him to retreat into his phone, scrolling endlessly through social media, playing video games, or binge-watching light television as a way to avoid thinking about the assault. The more he avoided, the more he felt the urge to escape, and his phone screen became a lifeline that kept the terrifying images at bay. In this way, the triggers fed directly into his maladaptive strategies, which in turn fed the very triggers they sought to silence. At the same time, Kai's negative appraisals grew louder. The image of himself as a "victim" of a random attacker made him blame his own character-he was certain that his rough, unkempt appearance or the fact that he worked late nights had invited the assault. He told himself he had no future, that his life was a series of random misfortunes, and that if someone else had been in his shoes, they would not have been caught in the same predicaments. These thoughts amplified his sense of threat: he was constantly on edge, startle-prone to any sudden movement or unexpected touch, and he avoided unfamiliar places such as the new construction sites his coworkers asked him to visit. He feared that any new environment could harbor another intruder, and his heart would race even before he set foot in an unfamiliar hallway. The weight of hopelessness and self-blame turned his sense of danger into a pervasive, almost inevitable feeling that everything around him could become the next assault. The traumatic memory itself acted like a mirror that reflected back to Kai the same triggers, the same threat, and the same negative thoughts. He could recall the assault as a series of isolated snapshots-dark silhouettes, the knife's glare, the hiss of the door-each fragment a picture he could not piece together into a coherent story. The incomplete nature of the memory left him with a gnawing sense that something was missing; each time he tried to reconstruct the event, a new piece of the puzzle surfaced, causing him to feel guilty for not remembering it fully. That guilt pushed him to screen-escape, to drink beer after a long shift, and to use prescription medication to numb the pain. In each instance of avoidance, the negative appraisal that "I am a weak, guilty man" intensified, reinforcing the sense that he was constantly threatened by danger, which in turn drove him to use maladaptive strategies as a way to regain control. In his workshop, when a colleague asked him to examine a newly installed panel in a building he had never worked on, Kai's body tightened. He imagined a stranger standing beside him, a knife flashing in the weak light, and a door slamming behind them. His hands trembled, his vision blurred, and he fled the job, leaving the toolboxes behind. The avoidance of that unfamiliar place forced him to miss out on a promotion he had been hoping for, reinforcing his belief that a future was impossible. Each missed opportunity fed the same negative appraisal: "I'm doomed to fail because I'm not strong enough." The loop tightened until Kai could no longer ignore the fear. Only when his wife's concern for his health-she had watched him stumble home after a long shift, his shoulders hunched, his face pale-reached a breaking point did he finally seek help. Kai feared that if he did not intervene, the next time he stepped through a door he would lose his life again. He hopes that by confronting the triggers and the memories, he might regain a sense of safety and reconnect with his job, his wife, and his future.
